title: Rubio Calls India Important Ally as Trump Pauses Russia Sanctions Tariffs
excerpt: Trump waived Graham Act duties that could have hit India with up to 100% tariffs over Russian oil purchases, giving Washington a 60-day review and New Delhi immediate relief.
body:
• President Donald Trump has waived key Russia sanctions and tariffs under the Graham Act, pausing duties that were due to take effect on Sunday.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio called India an "important ally and partner" and said New Delhi has diversified its energy portfolio but cannot pivot away from Russian supply in a day.
  • The law would have allowed tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian crude and gas, including India and China.
  • For Indian exporters and refiners, the waiver removes an immediate tariff threat for a 60-day review period while Washington studies the impact on the global and US economies.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has defended President Donald Trump’s decision to waive Russia-related sanctions, calling India an important ally whose energy needs must be considered before tariffs are imposed. Speaking on Saturday, a day after Trump signed the waiver, Rubio said the administration wants a 60-day period to analyse what sanctions and tariffs would mean for the global economy and for the United States itself.

"These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries — India, for example, and others," Rubio said, according to ANI reporting carried by New Kerala and Live Mint.

"You've got countries like India, for example, that have voluntarily diversified their energy portfolio, but are still getting a substantial amount of energy from Russia because it's hard to pivot from one day to the next."

— Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State

What the waiver actually does

The mechanism is a presidential waiver under Section 115 of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act. That section allows the president to waive sanctions, restrictions and duties in the Act if he certifies to Congress that doing so is in the national interest of the United States, with a report explaining the basis. Trump invoked that provision on Friday, waiving duties under sections 112 and 113 — provisions that would have allowed duties of up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on goods from the five largest importers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas. The waiver continues until the president or the secretary of state decides further action is warranted, in consultation with the Treasury secretary and the US trade representative. In practice, India and other large Russian-oil buyers keep selling into the US market without the new punitive duty while the review runs.

Why Washington paused

Rubio said the waiver provisions were written into the Act precisely because lawmakers understood conditions could change. He pointed to pressure on global energy supplies from the war involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, and damage to energy infrastructure in the Russia-Ukraine war. Imposing sweeping tariffs in that environment, he argued, could lift global prices and hurt the US economy as well as allies.

He also rejected the suggestion that the waiver, alongside a separate arrangement for Russian diesel, amounted to a concession to Moscow. That diesel, he said, was going to be sold one way or the other. New Kerala reported Trump announced Russia would supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tonnes during November and 1 million tonnes thereafter.

What it means for India

India is one of the world’s largest buyers of Russian crude, and its refiners — including the complex at Jamnagar, which Rubio is scheduled to visit — have built supply chains around discounted Russian barrels since 2022. An abrupt 100% tariff on Indian goods would have hit exporters far beyond energy, from pharmaceuticals to textiles, for a sourcing decision refiners cannot reverse overnight. Rubio’s language acknowledges that reality: India has diversified, he said, but still draws a substantial share of its energy from Russia.

Rubio is due in India on October 20 as part of a trip that also includes Uzbekistan, his second official visit to India this year after a May trip. Discussions in Mumbai and Jamnagar are expected to focus on bilateral ties, energy cooperation and commercial investment, according to the reports.

What happens next

The 60-day review is now the decision window. The administration must weigh whether reimposing the Graham Act duties would pressure Russia without destabilising energy markets or penalising partners it is courting in Asia. For New Delhi, the relief is real but temporary in design — the waiver can be ended by a further determination, and the underlying law remains on the books. Indian officials and exporters will be watching Rubio’s visit for any signal on whether the pause becomes a longer arrangement or a bridge to tougher terms.
